title: round(2.675, 2) is 2.67 in Python, not 2.68
assumption: round(x, 2) rounds a price to the nearest cent the way a calculator would, based on the decimal digits you wrote.

input.description: Rounding a unit price quoted to three decimals, such as $2.675 from a supplier price list or a per-unit rate table, to the nearest cent before storing or displaying it.

what_goes_wrong: `round(2.675, 2)` returns 2.67, not 2.68, even though 2.675 looks exactly halfway between 2.67 and 2.68.
why: The literal 2.675 is not exactly representable in IEEE-754 double; the nearest representable double is approximately 2.67499999999999982236..., which is strictly below the true halfway point. Python's round() rounds that actual stored value, so it correctly rounds down to 2.67 - the "error" is in the input's binary representation, not in round()'s rounding rule. This is the same mechanism as JavaScript's toFixed surprises, and it is independent of Python's round-half-to-even tie-breaking rule, because 2.67499999999999982236... isn't a tie to begin with.
affects: any IEEE-754 double rounded by value rather than by decimal text

repros.code:
x = 2.675
print(round(x, 2))
print(f"{x:.20f}")
import decimal
print(decimal.Decimal(x))

fix: Build the number from a decimal string with decimal.Decimal("2.675") instead of a float literal, and round that - Decimal preserves the exact decimal value, so round-half-even on it gives the answer a human expects. Or round integer cents directly, never a float dollar amount.

sources.title: Python docs: 15.1. Floating-Point Arithmetic: Issues and Limitations

test_cases.note: A price-rounding function given the exact decimal string "2.675" should round to "2.68" (round-half-up on the true decimal value); round(float("2.675"), 2) in Python returns 2.67 instead.
